$comment: The sweep: flatten everything the hand-written manifest does not cover.
The official ArtAssetID dictionary dates from 2007 and lists ~180 assets.
A real modern skin replaces ~2600. Covering only the documented ones
repaints about 5% of the interface, which reads as 'nothing changed'.
So: skin/dictionary.txt holds the full ID list, and these ordered rules
assign each one a flat colour. First match wins. Anything matching an
Every sweep asset is a SOLID FILL with no border and no 9-slice detail.
That is deliberate: a solid colour looks identical whether the client
stretches, tiles or crops it, so we do not need to know the dimension the
game expects. Assets where a border or a corner actually matters live in
assets.json with their documented size and always take precedence.
Because the fills are solid, all IDs sharing a role point at ONE file.
$excludeComment: Pictograms and state colours. Flattening these would destroy information:
you would lose quest difficulty, item rarity, class resource pips and
The toolbar families below matter more than they look. In LOTRO a button
like bag1_normal IS its own picture -- there is no separate icon drawn
on top of a frame. Clearing it does not strip ornament, it deletes the
button. That is what made the bag, journal and map buttons vanish.
$rulesComment: Ordered, first match wins. `color` and `opacity` are theme roles; an
opacity of 0 produces a fully transparent file.
THE GOVERNING RULE: removing ornament means making it INVISIBLE, not
painting a dark rectangle over it. An opaque fill on an unknown asset
covers whatever the client draws underneath, which is how you end up with
black blocks over portraits and action bar buttons.
So only assets we can positively identify as a background get a fill.
Everything else becomes transparent: worst case something decorative
disappears, which is the goal, and nothing can ever obscure content.

rules.$note: Hover feedback. Kept, because losing it makes the UI feel dead.
Pressed feedback, a touch darker than hover

$note: Actual backgrounds. This is the only group that gets an opaque-ish
fill, and it is what replaces the carved stone behind the vitals,
the character panel and the journals.
Clickable surfaces need to stay visible. A transparent button is an
invisible button, which is worse than an ornate one. These get a
translucent plate: clearly a control, never a black slab.

rules.$note: Rules and separators stay visible as a hairline

$note: Everything else: frames, corners, end caps, filigree, plates, the
ornate chrome around every panel. This is the bulk of what makes
LOTRO's UI look busy, and all of it simply goes away.
